newsitem.title: USA: Mud disposal site approved for New York Harbor.
newsitem.headline: Mud disposal site approved for New York Harbor.

text.p: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said Friday it had granted a permit to the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey to begin construction of three underwater pits that will hold polluted mud dredged from the harbor's shipping channels.

Approval of the project, which had been expected, marks a crucial step forward in the port's effort to clear the harbor's clogged berths and channels before a key offshore dump site closes in September, officials said.

"This federal approval achieves a major milestone in the continuing effort to provide an environmentally responsible disposal site for dredged muds unsuitable for ocean disposal," the Army Corps said in a statement.
"The lack of disposal sites for dredged material has imperiled the Port's economic viability."

The three underwater pits, which combined will span 31 acres on the New Jersey side of the port in Newark Bay, will hold some 3.1 million cubic yards of mud deemed too unsafe to be dumped into the open ocean.
Construction is expected to begin in late May or early June.
Left alone, New York's naturally shallow shipping lanes would silt up to a depth of around 20 feet, rendering them impassable to modern commercial vessels.

The harbor has been dredged in one form or another for more than a century, but with a ban on ocean dumping of polluted mud set to go into effect on September 1, port officials have raced to come up alternative disposal sites.
Meanwhile, dredging projects stalled as various groups debated how to balance commercial and ecological interests in the harbor.

But earlier this month, state and federal officials, along with environmentalists and labor leaders, announced that they had effectively buried the hatchet and would work together to keep the harbor open while protecting the surrounding environment.

The Newark Bay site, which will be filled to capacity in anywhere from one to three years, is seen largely as a stop-gap measure to keep the port operable while longer-term dredging and disposal options are explored.
((-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
